name: Peach Tree of the Queen Mother of the West
native: 西王母桃樹 · xī wángmǔ táo shù
era: Zhou dynasty sources (1st millennium BCE); Han codification
story: On Mount Yaoqi in the western reaches, the Queen Mother of the West (Xiwangmu) keeps a garden of three peach trees. Each tree bears fruit only once every three thousand years, and a single bite of the golden peach grants immortality. When the immortal Zhongli Qu, who had already eaten three peaches in a lifetime, sneaks back for a fourth, the Queen Mother exposes him, and he withers to an infant in her court.
history: Xiwangmu first appears in the Zhou-dynasty text Mountain and Sea Classic (Shan Hai Jing) as a half-human, half-beast guardian, and by the Han dynasty she had become a fully divine matriarch of the immortal isles. The peach became China's foremost longevity symbol: the 'peach banquet' (taohui) celebrating a long-lived elder is still the standard birthday honor for the elderly, and peaches are the default offering at longevity festivals.
details: The three thousand-year fruiting cycle encodes a cosmology of time: the mortal realm ages in years while the immortal garden ages in epochs. Peaches are also apotropaic — door gods hold them, and the peach-blossom sword is the archetypal weapon against ghosts. The fruit's duality (immortality and exorcism) makes the peach tree the most functional sacred tree in Chinese religion.
sources: Shan Hai Jing (Mountain and Sea Classic), esp. Guo Zhu's 3rd-c. commentary
Legge, James. The Mountains and Seas (1882 translation)
Mair, Victor H. The Mountain and Sea Classics (1993)

name: Jing, the Axis Tree of Heaven
era: Pre-Qin sources; attested in Shan Hai Jing
story: In the oldest Chinese cosmography, a great luminous tree called the Jing stands at the navel of the world. The sun, the moon, and the stars circle or ascend it; the gods gather beneath it, and the emperor's capital is said to mirror its axis. It is the tree through which the celestial and the terrestrial realms are joined — the original Chinese world tree, preceding the later Meru-derived imagery of Buddhism.
history: The Jing appears in early chapters of the Shan Hai Jing, where it is associated with the sun god and with the emperor's sacred precincts. Later Han and Tang ritual commentaries identified it with the 'central tree' of the imperial capital — the axis about which the palace grid was oriented. When Buddhist Mount Meru entered Chinese cosmology from the 4th century, the Jing's role as vertical axis was largely absorbed into the Meru image, but the word survived in ritual and poetic registers.
details: Unlike the more narrative trees of Chinese myth, the Jing is pure structure: it is the axis mundi itself. Its name is etymologically linked to 'jing' meaning splendor and to the sun's brightness, which is why the tree is described as radiant even before the sun reaches it. It is the closest Chinese parallel to Yggdrasil in function — the pillar that holds heaven, earth, and the underworld in one column.
sources: Shan Hai Jing (Mountain and Sea Classic)
Mair, Victor H. The Mountain and Sea Classics (1993)
Saso, Michael. The Tree of God in Chinese Mythology (study of jing cosmography)

name: Jade Tree of the Immortal Isles
tree: Jade / crystal (mythic material, not a species)
story: In the islands of the eastern sea where immortals dwell, trees grow of living jade: their branches are polished emerald, their fruit pearls and jade seeds. To eat a single fruit is to shed the mortal body. Wanderers who stumble on the isles — fishermen, shipwrecked officials — are tempted, and those who eat the jade fruit are never seen in the mortal world again.
history: The jade tree (yushu) recurs in Han dynasty immortality literature and in the Shan Hai Jing's accounts of the eastern sea isles. 'Jade tree' also became a fixed literary and artistic formula — a phrase for any tree of supernatural beauty in poetry, and a standard motif in Tang and Song painting of immortal landscapes. The material matters: jade was the substance of incorruptibility in Chinese belief, so a tree of it is a tree that cannot decay.
details: Where the peach tree of Xiwangmu grants life through fruit eaten in time, the jade tree grants it through substance itself — the whole tree is immortal because it is made of the incorruptible mineral. It sits at the other end of Chinese immortal botany: not a tree that gives life, but a tree that is already life made solid. The motif survives in the phrase 'jade tree and jade stone' for refined, otherworldly beauty.
sources: Shan Hai Jing (Mountain and Sea Classic)
Mair, Victor H. The Mountain and Sea Classics (1993)
Standard Tang/Song painting motif catalogues

name: Longevity Trees of Penglai
native: 蓬萊長生樹 · pénglái chángshēng shù
era: Qin–Han (seeking by Qin Shi Huang, 3rd c. BCE onward)
tree: Mixed immortal flora (peach, jade, and unnamed changsheng trees)
story: Penglai, one of the three great islands floating in the eastern sea, is home to the Queen Mother's kin and to trees of endless life (changsheng shu). Emperor Qin Shi Huang, terrified of death, dispatched the envoy Xu Fu with thousands of youths and maidens to sail east and find the islands' fruit that would make him immortal. Xu Fu never returned. The search set a pattern: every Han emperor after him sent expeditions east for the same trees.
history: Penglai's fame is fixed by the Qin and Han imperial searches recorded by Sima Qian (Records of the Grand Historian). The islands' location kept receding as sailors approached — a narrative device encoding their otherworldliness. The longing for Penglai became a whole genre of Chinese poetry and landscape painting, and the name Penglai (a real coastal city) carried the myth into place-names across the northern coast.
details: The changsheng shu ('long-life tree') is a category, not a species — anything that does not die. The island's trees are the destination of the most famous imperial quest in Chinese history, which is why Penglai sits at the center of the immortality imagination. The myth also seeded the Japanese and Korean 'island of the immortals' (shinsen / shinsan) traditions, traveling with maritime contact.
sources: Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji), ch. 28
Mair, Victor H. The Mountain and Sea Classics (1993)

name: Sacred Nagi of the Sun Shrine
native: 神渕の杜 · kamiizumi no mori; 神木 · kamiboki
era: Mythic antiquity; shrine rebuilt every 20 years since at least the 7th c. CE
story: At Ise, the inner shrine of Amaterasu (the sun goddess) is surrounded by a grove of sacred nagi trees, and a single great nagi stands as the kami's dwelling-tree. Every twenty years the entire shrine — and the grove's central tree — is ceremonially rebuilt in an identical copy (shikinen sengu). The tree is not worshipped as an object but treated as the living presence of the goddess's dwelling, renewed in perpetuity so that the shrine never grows old.
history: The Ise shrines' ritual of periodic rebuilding (shikinen sengu) is the oldest continuously practiced ritual in the world, running unbroken for over a thousand years. The nagi was chosen as the sacred species of the shrine: it is evergreen, aromatic, and its wood was used for the shrine's most sacred components. The practice encodes a theology of perpetual renewal — the sacred is kept alive by being constantly recreated, never allowed to fossilize into a monument.
details: The nagi's role is architectural as much as spiritual: it is the tree that houses the deity. Its aromatic wood was believed to ward off decay and evil, which is why it was used for the shrine's sacred objects. The twenty-year cycle makes the nagi a living metronome of the shrine's time — each generation of Japanese knows the grove as newly planted, so the sacred tree is forever young.
sources: Ise Jingu official ritual records (shikinen sengu)
Pott, John. The Ise Shrines and Shikinen Sengu (study of the renewal ritual)

name: Sacred Fig of Isonokami
native: 伊佐那岐の樹 · isonokami no ki
era: Mythic antiquity; shrine attested by 8th c. CE (Kojiki, Nihon Shoki)
story: When the sun goddess Amaterasu left the Heavenly Plain to found the realm of mortals, she alighted upon a great fig tree on the island of Izumo, where the deity Isonokami awaited her. That tree — the isonokami — marks the exact spot where the divine descended to earth, and it became the most sacred fig in Japan. To stand beneath it is to stand at the hinge between the heavenly and the human worlds.
history: The descent of Amaterasu onto the fig at Isonokami is recorded in the two oldest Japanese chronicles, the Kojiki (712) and the Nihon Shoki (720). The site at Kashima / Izumo became a major shrine, and the sacred fig (ichii) was recognized across Japan as a tree of divine descent and of the founding of place. Figs in general became associated with the establishment of sacred ground — a fig marks where a kami has landed.
details: The fig's role is locative: it fixes the myth in a place. Unlike the nagi that houses the deity in a shrine, the isonokami fig marks the moment the deity left the sky. It is the tree of foundation — the point of contact between the celestial and the terrestrial — which is why figs so often stand at the centers of Japanese sacred sites and at the roots of shrine groves.
sources: Kojiki (712), Nihon Shoki (720) — descent narratives
Standard Shinto shrine-tree catalogues (ichii as sacred fig)

name: Dado, the World Tree of Heaven
era: Pre-Buddist Korean cosmology; attested in early mythic sources
tree: Unspecified great tree (described as spanning heaven, earth, and underworld)
story: In the oldest Korean cosmology, a colossal tree called Dado stands at the center of the world. Its crown reaches the heavens, its trunk passes through the earth, and its roots plunge into the underworld. The three realms — heaven, the human world, and the realm of the dead — are the three levels of a single tree, and the spirits of the dead climb its roots while the gods dwell in its branches. It is the original Korean axis mundi, the pillar that holds the cosmos upright.
history: Dado appears in pre-Budd Korean creation and cosmological traditions and in the mythology surrounding the founding of the Korean people. When Buddhism arrived (4th–6th c. CE), the image of Dado was partially fused with the Buddhist Mount Meru and with the Bodhi tree of enlightenment, but the native Dado survived in folk cosmology, in the ritual language of shamans (mudang), and in the imagery of Korean shamanism as the tree connecting the three worlds.
details: Dado's function is purely structural — it is the tree that makes the three realms into one connected place. Its roots in the underworld and crown in heaven make it the elevator between life and death, which is why Korean shamanic ritual so often invokes climbing or descending a great tree to carry messages between the living and the dead. It is the Korean counterpart to Yggdrasil and the Mesoamerican ceiba.
sources: Korean shamanic (mudang) ritual tradition
Studies of pre-Buddhist Korean cosmology and Dado myth

name: Champa Tree of the Samye Dream
native: ཇམ་པའི་མེ་ཏོག · jampa'i metok; 金盞花 · jīnzhǎnhuā
story: King Trisong Detsen, founder of Tibetan Buddhism, dreamed of a great champa tree in full bloom on a hill above the future site of Samye, the first monastery in Tibet. In the dream, the tree's fragrance announced that the Indian masters who would bring the Dharma were already on their way. When the Indian pandits Sarodharma and Vairotsana arrived and the monastery was built, the champa tree was said to bloom out of season in confirmation of the dream — the tree became the living seal that the prophecy was true.
history: The champa (cempaka) tree was already sacred in Indian and Southeast Asian tradition as a tree of fragrance and of the gods. In the Samye narrative it becomes the botanical proof of prophecy — a tree that blooms on the king's command to validate the arrival of Buddhism. The dream-and-blossom story is a founding text of Tibetan monastic history and is still retold at Samye. The champa remains a flower of high sanctity in Tibetan ritual garlands (phundru).
details: The champa's power here is olfactory and prophetic: its fragrance is the sign, and its out-of-season bloom is the miracle. It is less a world tree than a verification tree — a plant that testifies. That is why the cempaka/champa appears so often in Himalayan ritual as the flower of consecration: it is the tree that confirms the sacred has arrived.
sources: Tibetan monastic histories of Samye (e.g., the bKa'-'gyur founding texts)
Studies of Trisong Detsen and the introduction of Buddhism to Tibet

name: Ukhai, the Sacred Tree of the Steppe
tree: Usually oak, elm, or poplar (whatever great tree the clan chose)
story: Every Mongol clan and many steppe villages keep an ukhai — a single great tree set apart as the dwelling of the clan's spirit and the axis of its territory. Riders dismount and circle it; offerings of silk (khadag) are tied to its branches; and the tree's health is read as the health of the clan. To cut an ukhai is the gravest of desecrations, an offense against the clan's own spirit.
history: The ukhai tradition is a core institution of pre-Buddhist Mongol shamanism and survives alongside (and often beneath) the later Buddhist layer. It is the steppe expression of a very wide Eurasian pattern — the sacred tree as clan axis — seen also among the Turkic and Tungus peoples. Even after the mass conversion to Buddhism and then to state atheism, the ukhai persisted in rural practice, and today it is a visible part of the steppe landscape and of revived shamanic ceremony.
details: The ukhai is a territorial and genealogical marker as much as a spiritual one: it defines where the clan's spirit lives and therefore where the clan's land begins. Its branches, heavy with blue silk scarves, are a recognizable sight across Mongolia. The tree is the clan's living ancestor, the fixed point around which the mobile steppe life organizes itself.
symbolism: the fixed point of the steppe
sources: Mongol shamanic (böö) tradition
Ethnographic studies of Mongol sacred trees (ukhai) and steppe ritual

name: Kuyaa, the Sacred Tree of the Ryukyuan Villages
era: Ryukyu Kingdom period (15th–19th c.); continuous to present
tree: Varies — often camphor, banyan, or a great native tree
story: In the villages of the Ryukyu islands, a chosen great tree is the kuyaa — the dwelling-place of the village's guardian spirit (the mifu or a local kami) and the axis of the community's ritual life. Before harvests, before building, and before any communal undertaking, the villagers offer rice, sake, and prayers at the kuyaa. The tree is the village's spiritual elder, the one whose blessing makes the community's work lawful.
history: The kuyaa is a central feature of Ryukyuan (Okinawan) indigenous religion, which retained a strong animist and spirit-dwelling layer even under the later Confucian and Japanese influences of the Ryukyu Kingdom. The tradition is part of the broader East Asian pattern of the village sacred tree, and in Okinawa it survives as a living practice: many villages still maintain a kuyaa and hold offerings at it. The Okinawan concept of the sacred tree is closely tied to the idea of the 'sacred grove' (the mifu's domain) at the village edge.
details: The kuyaa is a community tree, not an individual's — it belongs to the village and its guardian spirit. Its role is to mediate between the human community and the spirit world, making the village's collective actions ritually valid. It is the Okinawan counterpart to the Mongol ukhai and the Vietnamese village banyan: the tree that anchors a community's spirit to a place.
sources: Ryukyuan (Okinawan) indigenous religious tradition (mifu and kuyaa)
Ethnographic studies of Okinawan village sacred trees

name: Cây Đa, the Sacred Banyan of the Village
story: At the center or edge of a Vietnamese village stands the great banyan (cây đa), whose aerial roots and wide canopy make it a tree that is also a place. Beneath it the elders meet, disputes are settled, and the village's guardian spirit (the thành hoàng) is honored. The banyan is the village's living meeting hall and its spiritual axis — to sit in its shade is to sit in the company of the village's own spirit and of its ancestors.
history: The banyan's centrality in Vietnamese village life is ancient and continuous. It is the physical focus of the thành hoàng worship (village guardian cult) and of communal decision-making. The image of the great banyan is so fundamental to Vietnamese village identity that it appears in folk song, in the iconography of the village, and in the very layout of the settlement. The tree's capacity to make new trunks from its aerial roots made it a natural symbol of the village's self-renewing continuity.
details: The banyan is a tree that contains a community: its shade is the village's public space, its spirit is the village's guardian, and its endless rooting is the village's continuity. It is one of the most concrete expressions of the East Asian 'village sacred tree' pattern — the tree that makes a cluster of houses into a place with a soul.
sources: Vietnamese village (làng) tradition and thành hoàng worship
Ethnographic studies of Vietnamese village sacred trees (cây đa)

name: Bamboo Stalk of Malakas at Maguayan
era: Oral tradition; recorded in the 17th c. and later
story: In the Tagalog origin myth, the first man and woman, Malakas and Maguayan, were not born of clay or of a woman's body but of a bamboo stalk. A young man shoots an arrow at a bamboo; the stalk splits, and from it emerge a man and a woman — the first people. They argue about who will rule the world, and from their contest the world is shaped. The bamboo, a tree-like grass, is thus the womb of humanity itself.
history: The bamboo origin myth is one of the most widespread creation narratives in the Philippines, with variants across Tagalog, Cebuano, and other Philippine languages. It was recorded by Spanish-era chroniclers and has been passed down orally ever since. The myth is a 'plant-womb' creation story — a type found across Island Southeast Asia — in which humanity emerges from a plant rather than from earth or from a divine parent.
details: The choice of bamboo is culturally precise: bamboo is the most useful and most sacred of Philippine plants, the material of houses, boats, and instruments, and a symbol of flexibility and resilience. Making humanity out of bamboo is to make them of the most vital and useful material in the world. The myth encodes a botany of origin — people are plant-born, and the plant world is their elder sibling.
sources: Tagalog and Philippine creation mythology (oral tradition)
Spanish-era chronicles of Philippine myths; modern collections of Philippine folklore

name: Sacred Phi Tree of the Thai Village
native: ต้นไม้ศักดิ์สิทธิ์ · nong mai sakchit (sacred tree)
tree: Varies — often banyan, mango, or a great native tree
story: Thai villages and households keep sacred trees in which phi (spirits) dwell — the guardian spirit of the village, the spirit of a place, or the spirit of an ancestor. Offerings of flowers, incense, food, and cloth are made at the tree, and the phi's favor is sought before planting, building, or traveling. The tree is the spirit's body: harm the tree and you harm the spirit; honor the tree and you are protected.
history: The worship of phi in trees is a deep layer of Thai religion, underlying and coexisting with Theravada Buddhism. The sacred tree (nong mai sakchit) is a standard feature of Thai village life and of the household altar. The practice is part of the broader Southeast Asian pattern of spirit-dwelling trees seen across mainland and island Southeast Asia, and it persists in modern Thailand alongside Buddhist practice.
details: The phi tree is a practical as well as a spiritual institution: it is where the community negotiates with the spirit world for protection and prosperity. The tree's specific species is less important than its age, size, and the spirit believed to inhabit it. It is the Thai expression of the widespread belief that a great old tree is a dwelling, not merely a plant.
sources: Thai phi (spirit) worship tradition
Ethnographic studies of Thai village sacred trees (nong mai sakchit)

name: Living Banyans of Angkor
native: ប្រាសាទអង្គរ · the temples of Angkor
era: Temple period (9th–15th c.); trees growing since then
story: At Angkor, great banyans and strangler figs have grown through and around the temple ruins for centuries, their roots wrapping the stone like hands around a body. At Ta Prohm and elsewhere, the trees and the temple have become a single structure: the banyan is both the destroyer and the consecrator of the sacred place. The Khmer built their temples as dwellings for the gods, and the banyans — themselves trees of spirit-dwelling — have simply continued that vocation, taking the stone for their own.
history: The banyan was already sacred in Khmer and wider Southeast Asian tradition as a spirit-dwelling and a village tree. When the Angkor temples were abandoned (from the 15th c.), the banyans that had grown in and around them — likely already venerated — completed the fusion of tree and temple. Today the image of the banyan-strangled temple is the defining visual of Angkor and of Khmer spiritual landscape, a physical record of the tree's ancient sacred status reclaiming human stone.
details: The Angkor banyans are a literal enactment of the sacred tree's power: the tree does not merely symbolize the divine dwelling, it becomes one, absorbing the human attempt to build a dwelling for the gods. The roots that crack the stone are the same roots that, in village belief, anchor a spirit to the earth. The temple is a tree's house as much as a god's.
sources: Angkor / Ta Prohm temple complex (UNESCO World Heritage)
Khmer banyan (spirit-dwelling tree) tradition

name: Great Tree of the Sky God Kaum Kaet
native: កូមកែត · Kaum Kaet
tree: Unnamed great tree of the sky
story: In Khmer cosmology, the sky god Kaum Kaet (a form of the Hindu Indra) dwells in the heavens and is associated with a great tree whose fruit grants power and sovereignty. The god is depicted seated on the elephant Airavata, and his tree is the source of the authority that kings claim by divine right. To possess the fruit of the sky god's tree is to possess the right to rule — the tree is the botanical root of kingship itself.
history: Kaum Kaet is one of the principal deities of Khmer folk cosmology, a native form of the Hindu Indra who survived the transition from Hindu-Buddhist state religion to Theravada Buddhism. His association with a great tree of power is part of the Khmer divine-kingship (devaraja) ideology, in which the king's authority was derived from the gods. The tree is thus less a mythic plant than a symbol of the divine source of political power in the Khmer world.
details: The sky god's tree encodes a theology of sovereignty: power is not seized but eaten, taken from the fruit of a tree that belongs to the sky god. It is the Khmer expression of a widespread idea that legitimate rule is a divine gift, and that the tree — the axis of the world — is the channel through which that gift descends. It sits at the intersection of cosmology, kingship, and botany.
sources: Khmer devaraja (divine kingship) tradition
Khmer folk cosmology and Kaum Kaet (Indra) worship

name: World Tree and Naga of the Dayak
era: Oral tradition; recorded from the 19th c.
story: In the cosmology of the Dayak peoples of Borneo, a great world tree stands at the center of creation, connecting the upper world of the gods, the middle world of humans, and the lower world of the dead. Coiled around the trunk is a great naga (serpent), whose body is the ring that binds the three realms together. The first human was shaped and placed at the foot of the tree, and the tree and the naga together are the frame within which all life — human, animal, and spirit — is ordered.
history: The Dayak world-tree-and-naga cosmology is one of the great creation narratives of Island Southeast Asia, shared in variant forms across the Dayak groups (Kenyah, Kenoyan, Bidayuh, Iban, and others) of Borneo. It was recorded by colonial-era ethnographers and survives in the ritual language of the traditional Dayak priests (lemang / bangsor). The cosmology is part of the wider Austronesian and Bornean pattern of the world tree, and it sits alongside the naga/serpent motif that runs across Southeast Asian cosmology.
details: The distinctive feature of the Dayak cosmology is the naga coiled around the tree: the tree is the vertical axis, the serpent is the horizontal binding that holds the three worlds in place. Together they form a cosmic loom — the structure within which life is woven. It is one of the most complete 'axis + binding' cosmologies in the world, a precise structural myth rather than a narrative one.
sources: Dayak (Bornean) creation cosmology (oral tradition)
Ethnographic studies of Dayak (Kenyah/Kenoyan/Bidayuh) world-tree and naga cosmology

name: Sacred Spirit Trees of Java
tree: Varies — often banyan, almond, or a great native tree
story: Across Java, certain great trees are the fixed dwellings of spirits (jihad / lelembut) who can possess a person (kerasukan) to deliver blessings, healing, or messages. Pilgrims travel to a specific sacred tree to be possessed by its spirit — to receive a cure, a prophecy, or a gift of strength. The tree is the spirit's anchor: the spirit is bound to that tree, and the pilgrim's journey is to the tree, not to a temple. The most famous of these is the tradition of the sacred trees of the Javanese spiritual landscape.
history: The kerasukan (possession) tradition and its sacred trees are a deep layer of Javanese spiritual life, underlying the official Islam and the older Hindu-Buddhist heritage. The practice is part of the broader Javanese (and wider Indonesian) pattern of spirit-dwelling trees, and it persists in modern Java as a living form of popular piety. The sacred trees are often old, large, and located at crossroads, riverbanks, or forest edges — the liminal places where the spirit world is thought to be thin.
details: The Javanese sacred tree is a site of direct spiritual contact: the tree is not merely honored but used as the point of entry for a spirit into a human body. This makes it a 'functional' sacred tree — a tree with a specific spiritual service (healing, prophecy, possession) rather than a purely symbolic one. It is one of the most active forms of tree-spirit worship in the world.
sources: Javanese kerasukan (possession) tradition
Ethnographic studies of Javanese sacred trees and spirit worship

name: Sacred Grove of the Balinese Village
tree: Mixed native forest (banyan, areca, and other sacred species)
story: Each Balinese village (banjar) keeps a sacred grove (wana) at its edge, a stand of trees that is the dwelling of the village's guardian spirits and of the gods. The grove is the village's spiritual boundary and its source of water and protection. No one cuts a tree in the grove; offerings are made at its threshold; and the grove is the living link between the village and the mountain (the direction of the sacred). To protect the grove is to protect the village.
history: The Balinese sacred grove is a central institution of Balinese Hindu village life, rooted in the Tri Hita Karana philosophy (harmony among humans, between humans and the divine, and between humans and nature). The grove is the physical expression of that third harmony — the living, protected relationship between the village and the natural world. It is part of the wider Balinese system of sacred landscapes (the concept of the 'sacred center' and the 'sacred boundary') and persists as a living practice in every Balinese village.
details: The Balinese grove is a community-managed sacred forest — a real, functioning institution of environmental and spiritual protection. It is the Balinese answer to the question of how a community keeps a piece of the wild alive and sacred: by making it the dwelling of the gods and the boundary of the village. It is one of the most successful examples in the world of a sacred tree/grove tradition that also functions as conservation.
sources: Balinese Hindu village (banjar) tradition and Tri Hita Karana philosophy
Ethnographic studies of Balinese sacred groves (wana)

name: Sacred Trees of the Myanmar Nats
native: နတ် · nat (spirit); သစ် · tree
tree: Varies — each nat is associated with a specific tree or grove
story: In Myanmar, the 37 nats (powerful spirits) — and countless local nats — are each associated with a sacred tree or grove where they dwell and where offerings are made. A nat's tree is its body and its throne: to honor the nat, one honors the tree. The nats are the spirits of ancestors, of heroes, and of the natural world, and their trees are the fixed points of their power. Pilgrims travel to a nat's tree to make merit, to seek protection, and to negotiate with the spirit for prosperity and safety.
history: Nat worship is the indigenous spiritual layer of Burmese religion, coexisting with (and predating) Theravada Buddhism. The 37 nats were formally recognized and ordered in the 19th century (under King Bagyidaw), but the worship of nat-spirits in trees is far older. The tradition is a core part of Burmese popular religion, and the sacred trees of the nats are a visible and active part of the Burmese landscape and ritual life. It is part of the wider Southeast Asian pattern of spirit-dwelling trees.
details: The Myanmar nat tree is a personalized sacred tree: each nat has its own tree, its own character, and its own domain (some are spirits of the dead, some of nature, some of historical figures). This makes the nat tree a richly individualized form of the sacred-tree tradition — a tree with a name, a biography, and a personality, rather than a generic spirit-dwelling. It is one of the most elaborate systems of tree-spirit worship in the world.
sources: Myanmar nat (spirit) worship tradition and the 37 nats
Ethnographic studies of Burmese nat trees and spirit worship
